tldr: To improve imitation-learned visual navigation diffusion policies, this paper proposes GQRM—an RL post-training framework using goal-independent trajectory perturbations and per-state Q-score normalization—enabling multi-embodiment adaptation and the emergence of novel behaviors such as dead-end recovery.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of X-NavDP. Robot embeddings are injected into the diffusion backbone via FiLM layers, while exploration is driven by structural perturbations mixing goal-conditioned and goal-free predictions. Large-scale parallel reinforcement learning is performed via Group Q-score Reweighted Matching (GQRM), where scores are reweighted using Q-values normalized within the same state.
overview:
In visual navigation using large-scale simulation data, diffusion policies trained via imitation learning on oracle planner demonstrations have gained significant attention. However, real-world robots only have access to partial local observations from onboard cameras. Consequently, pure imitation learning fails to yield recovery behaviors—such as escaping dead ends or detouring around long obstacles—and struggles to adapt to the diverse kinematic constraints of different robot platforms.

Post-training with reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled remedy, but applying RL to diffusion models has traditionally yielded marginal improvements due to unstable likelihood estimation and inefficient exploration. To break through this barrier, this work proposes a data-efficient diffusion RL framework called Group Q-score Reweighted Matching (GQRM). Its key breakthroughs lie in combining self-bootstrapped exploration—which encourages diverse behaviors without destroying pretrained priors—with group Q-score normalization on each state, extracting effective learning signals even in challenging scenarios.

The authors built a large-scale parallel simulation environment in IsaacLab that runs differential-drive wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots simultaneously across 56 scenes during post-training. As a result, the fine-tuned policy drastically improved the navigation success rate from 61.20% to 84.28% in unseen simulation environments, and boosted success rates from 10% to 65% in difficult real-world scenarios such as dead-end recovery.
contributions: Proposed a self-bootstrapped trajectory perturbation method leveraging goal-independent predictions, prompting exploratory behaviors like backing out and wide detours without destroying the diffusion navigation policy's prior distribution.
Introduced GQRM, which performs reweighted score matching using Q-scores normalized within candidate groups per state, resolving the issue of vanishing learning signals in difficult states.

Combined lightweight robot embedding injection via FiLM layers with runtime temporal consistency guidance, enabling a single model to generalize across wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots while maintaining smooth real-world execution.
Demonstrated substantially higher navigation success rates and the emergence of novel behaviors over existing baselines across extensive simulations and experiments on three physical robot platforms.

sections.heading: Why Can't Imitation Learning Alone Escape Dead Ends?
sections.summary: Navigation policies trained by imitating oracle planners suffer from ambiguous decisions and a lack of recovery behaviors when deployed with partial local observations. While online RL post-training is promising, diffusion models suffer from training instability and poor exploration.
sections.details:
Pretraining general visual navigation policies based on diffusion models in large-scale simulation has recently seen great success. However, conventional imitation learning pipelines suffer from two fatal shortcomings.

The first is the gap between local observations and global demonstrations. During training, the model mimics optimal trajectories from an oracle planner with full access to a global map. Real robots, however, only perceive partial visual observations from onboard cameras. This discrepancy prevents the policy from learning trial-and-error failure-recovery capabilities, such as reversing out of dead ends or detouring around long obstacles.

The second is the neglect of embodiment dynamics. Training a single nominal trajectory without accounting for platform-specific kinematic constraints and dynamics causes behaviors to break down when ported across different robot forms.

Fine-tuning with reinforcement learning (RL) can bridge this gap, but applying RL to diffusion models faces technical hurdles. Policy gradient methods that backpropagate through long denoising chains (such as DPPO) suffer from extreme gradient instability, while methods that freeze the latent space restrict the policy from discovering flexible detour and reversal behaviors. Reweighted score matching approaches (such as DPMD) preserve pretrained knowledge well, but struggle on high-dimensional visual inputs and long-horizon navigation tasks.

This work addresses these challenges by introducing the Group Q-score Reweighted Matching (GQRM) framework, yielding X-NavDP—a policy that generalizes to novel behaviors and diverse embodiments through stable RL post-training.

sections.heading: Lineage of Navigation Diffusion Models and RL Fine-Tuning
sections.summary: While diffusion models are increasingly applied to robot control and navigation, online RL fine-tuning has faced a persistent tradeoff between stability and exploration. This work occupies a distinct position by uniting structural perturbation with group normalization.
sections.details:
This study relates to two main areas of research.

### 2.1 Diffusion Models for Robot Navigation
Diffusion models excel at capturing multimodal data distributions. Following the success of Diffusion Policy in manipulation, they have been extended to navigation. Prominent examples include NoMaD, which achieves multimodal goal prediction in image-goal navigation, and NavDP, which achieves high performance purely in simulation via a generate-and-filter pipeline. However, because these rely on imitation learning, their performance remains bounded by the quality and coverage of collected demonstrations.

### 2.2 Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Policies
Policy gradient methods that formulate the denoising process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), such as DDPO and DPPO, have been applied to image generation and robot control, but computational instability remains a constant issue. Conversely, DSRL optimizes only the initial noise, making it difficult to uncover new behaviors outside the pretraining distribution. Reweighted score matching methods like DPMD circumvent direct sampling from the intractable target distribution, but have not tackled navigation-specific exploration challenges.

Recent efforts attempt online RL fine-tuning on NavDP, yet their exploration relies solely on the inherent stochasticity of diffusion sampling, limiting behavioral diversity. This work stands apart by integrating structured trajectory perturbations, embodiment conditioning, and group Q-score normalization to boost both exploration efficiency and training stability simultaneously.

sections.heading: Foundations of Diffusion Navigation Policies and Policy Mirror Descent (DPMD)
sections.summary: Visual navigation is formulated as generating waypoint sequences conditioned on RGB-D observations and goals. This section reviews the Policy Kernel Mirror Descent (PMD) theoretical framework and DPMD's reweighted score matching objective for stable diffusion updates.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Diffusion Policies for Navigation
This work formulates navigation as receiving an observation $\mathbf{o}_t$ (such as an RGB-D image) and a goal specification $\mathbf{g}$, and iteratively denoising an action chunk $a^0 = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^H$ representing future waypoints. In the forward diffusion process, Gaussian noise is added, and the reverse process trains a noise prediction network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\phi$ via mean squared error (MSE) loss. During inference, denoising begins from random noise and outputs smooth trajectory chunks through the learned reverse process.

### 3.2 Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) and Diffusion Policy Mirror Descent (DPMD)
Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) is closely connected to trust-region methods like TRPO and PPO, regularizing each policy update with a KL divergence penalty. Given the current policy $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$ and state-action value function $Q(s, a)$, the update target has the closed-form solution $\pi_{\mathrm{MD}}(a|s) \propto \pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a|s) \exp(Q(s, a)/\lambda)$.

However, when the policy is a diffusion model, computing the partition function $Z_{\mathrm{MD}}(s)$ is intractable, preventing direct sampling from this target distribution. DPMD resolves this using reweighted score matching. By adding noise to actions $a_0$ sampled from the current policy and weighting the denoising score regression by $\exp(Q(s, a_0)/\lambda)$, the update increases the likelihood of high-value actions without requiring direct sampling from the intractable target distribution.

sections.heading: Three Core Designs of X-NavDP: Perturbation, GQRM, and Embodiment Modulation
sections.summary: Exploration is driven by structural perturbations leveraging pretrained model knowledge, while per-state Q-score normalization (GQRM) extracts learning gradients for escaping dead ends. FiLM-based embodiment conditioning and temporal guidance ensure smooth execution across robots.
sections.details:
The complete X-NavDP system is built on a large-scale parallel RL framework using IsaacLab. It adopts a hierarchical structure: the high-level diffusion policy outputs waypoint chunks 3 seconds into the future, Model Predictive Control (MPC) converts them into velocity commands, and low-level tracking controllers execute them at 25 Hz. This mechanism rests on three key components:

### 4.1 Self-Bootstrapped Perturbation
A goal-conditioned pretrained model generates trajectories pointing straight toward the goal and rarely explores recovery behaviors like reversing or lateral sidesteps on its own. Adding plain Gaussian noise, however, produces jagged trajectories that are physically unexecutable.
To overcome this, the authors leverage the pretrained model's goal-independent (NoGoal) branch. Denoising without a goal yields diverse, scene-compliant paths that navigate around local obstacles. By linearly interpolating this goal-free trajectory $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{\text{nogoal}}$ with the goal-conditioned trajectory $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{\text{pointgoal}}$, and probabilistically flipping lateral coordinates, the system produces diverse candidate trajectories—including detours and reversals—while preserving smooth, executable geometry.

### 4.2 GQRM: Group Q-score Reweighted Matching
Standard DPMD normalizes Q-values across the entire mini-batch. Consequently, easier states (with higher absolute Q-values) dominate the batch, washing out gradients in difficult states like dead ends where all candidates receive low Q-values.
GQRM instead computes the mean and standard deviation within the candidate group sampled from the exact same state, yielding a group-normalized Q-score $\widetilde{Q}_G(s, a_0)$. Even if absolute rewards are low, the best escape candidate within a dead end receives a substantially higher weight, providing a strong learning signal for recovery behaviors. Furthermore, updating only on top-ranked candidates with positive advantages reduces computation and suppresses noise.

### 4.3 Embodiment Modulation and Temporal Guidance
To support heterogeneous robots (wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid), a learnable robot ID embedding $\mathbf{z}_e$ is injected into the policy via token shifting before the decoder and FiLM modulation after the decoder. During deployment, a Real-Time Chunking (RTC)-inspired guidance objective penalizes deviations from the previously committed trajectory prefix, preventing control chattering and discontinuous motions.

sections.heading: Dramatic Traversability Gains and Novel Behaviors in Simulation and the Real World
sections.summary: Across 40 unseen scenes and three robot embodiments, X-NavDP improves success rates by over 23% compared to the baseline. In real-world tests without domain-specific tuning, hard-case success jumped from 10% to 65%, with clear emergence of novel behaviors like reversing and wide detours.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used realistic USD assets from GRScenes-100, with 56 scenes for training (47 residential, 9 commercial) and 40 completely unseen scenes for evaluation (20 residential, 20 commercial). Three robot embodiments were tested: Dingo (differential wheeled), Unitree Go2 (quadruped), and Unitree G1 (humanoid). Metrics include Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL). Physical experiments were conducted on Turtlebot, Go2, and G1 without additional Sim-to-Real fine-tuning.

### 5.2 Key Results
In simulation, the baseline NavDP achieved an average SR of 61.20% and SPL of 58.95%, whereas X-NavDP improved to an SR of 84.28% and SPL of 77.19%. The humanoid robot (G1)—which is tall and susceptible to tipping over—benefited most dramatically, jumping from 64.35% to 84.25% in commercial scenes and 50.70% to 84.50% in residential scenes.
In real-world deployment across challenging office and hallway environments with dead ends and extended obstacles, NavDP achieved only a 10% success rate, whereas X-NavDP reached 65%. As shown in Figure 3, the policy naturally exhibited reactive behaviors never present in the pretraining demonstrations: backing out of cul-de-sacs, circumnavigating long barriers, and choosing safer, wider corridors.

### 5.3 Ablation Studies and Failure Analysis
Comparing RL algorithms, policy gradient DPPO caused trajectory degradation and initial-noise optimization DSRL collapsed, whereas GQRM showed outstanding stability and performance. For exploration, removing self-bootstrapped perturbation caused training to collapse (SR plummeted to 6.23%), proving the necessity of structured candidate generation.
Remaining failure modes include physical arm collisions by the humanoid in tight spaces, loss of progress on very long walls where short-term memory expires and the robot loops back, and depth misestimations on transparent or mesh obstacles like glass and perforated partitions.

While NavDP gets stuck in dead ends, X-NavDP acquires behaviors such as backing out of traps (top), taking wide detours around extensive obstacles (middle), and selecting paths with larger safety margins (bottom).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: X-NavDP dramatically stabilizes and accelerates post-training of navigation diffusion policies via structured exploration and group-normalized score matching. Enhancing long-term memory and co-training with low-level locomotion remain exciting future directions.
sections.details:
This paper presented X-NavDP, an RL post-training framework that equips pretrained diffusion navigation models with novel behaviors and multi-embodiment adaptability. Combining self-bootstrapped perturbation from the model's own goal-free branch—without dedicated curiosity modules—with Group Q-score Reweighted Matching (GQRM) achieves remarkable data efficiency and training stability.

### Limitations and Future Directions
Currently, the policy relies on a short temporal context window, which can cause the robot to double back in complex, maze-like environments requiring long-term memory. Additionally, because the low-level locomotion controller is fixed, deploying to a new embodiment requires a pre-tuned low-level controller. Future work will explore extending this framework to Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) and establishing tighter end-to-end coordination between navigation and locomotion.

sections.heading: Appendix: Mathematical Derivation of GQRM and Reward Design
sections.summary: This section explains why per-state normalization succeeds in difficult states and details practical reinforcement learning setups, including A*-based progress rewards tailored to 3-second macro-steps.
sections.details:
### A. Derivation of GQRM and the Role of Per-State Normalization
In Denoising Score Matching (DSM), Tweedie's identity establishes that minimizing the MSE of a noise prediction network is equivalent to estimating the marginal score. DPMD leverages this framework to regress toward the PMD optimal policy distribution in score space. However, when weights $\exp(Q(s, a)/\lambda)$ are computed over the entire mini-batch, large Q-values from easy states are exponentially magnified, washing out the learning gradients of difficult states.
GQRM computes the mean $\bar{Q}_G(s)$ and standard deviation $\sigma_G(s)$ within the candidate group $\mathcal{G}(s)$ sampled from the exact same state $s$, and assigns weights using $\widetilde{Q}_G(s, a) = \mathrm{clip}(c (Q - \bar{Q}_G) / (\sigma_G + \varepsilon), -h, h)$. This ensures that even in cul-de-sacs where all candidates receive negative Q-values, local relative advantages are converted into meaningful learning signals.

### B. Reward Function and Training Schedule
RL transitions (macro-steps) are defined over 3-second execution intervals. The reward function combines a survival penalty (-0.025 per step), path progress based on A* search, goal arrival (stopping within 0.5 m for 4 seconds), collision penalties (contact forces exceeding 6.5 N), stagnation penalties (advancing less than 0.2 m over 6 seconds), and humanoid falling penalties. The progress reward uses A* costs on an occupancy grid incorporating obstacle clearance, rewarding trajectories that maintain safer margins from obstacles.

takeaways: In RL for diffusion policies, normalizing value functions within candidate groups sampled from the same state (GQRM)—rather than across the mini-batch—retains critical learning signals in hard states and stabilizes updates.
To explore without destroying pretrained priors, structured perturbation blending the model's own goal-free (NoGoal) branch is far more effective than adding pure Gaussian noise.
Injecting embodiment embeddings into the diffusion navigation policy via FiLM layers allows a single model to accommodate the kinematic differences of wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots.
Proper RL post-training naturally induces novel reactive behaviors never seen in imitation demonstrations, such as backing out of dead ends and taking wide detours.
limitations: Due to a short-term observation window, the policy can lose consistency and loop back when detouring around very long walls, revealing memory limitations.
The hierarchical architecture requires a pre-tuned low-level locomotion or base controller for each newly introduced embodiment.
RGB-D depth estimation degrades on transparent or hollow obstacles such as glass partitions and perforated metal screens, making the robot prone to collisions or getting stuck.
